sm: The hosts, Jenny Rough and Nick Eicher, open with a preview of the show: a ten percent Nasdaq plunge, a Supreme Court prisoner custody case, and the story of the Birdman of Alcatraz. Kent Covington then reports the news. The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of the National Crime Information Center, the database police use to check stolen cars and warrants. America's trade representative says new rules block Chinese firms from renting overseas computing power to train AI on advanced American chips. Democrats say President Trump is too friendly with Putin, while an intelligence official says Putin is not America's friend in Ukraine. Israel's opposition leader called settler arson attacks on West Bank villages Jewish terrorism, and 24 bodies were pulled from a capsized boat in Nigeria.

On the legal docket, the show covers a Supreme Court case involving federal prisoner William Maxwell, who is serving twenty years for racketeering and fraud. He says the government failed to credit time he earned under the First Step Act, which could move him to a halfway house or home confinement. The justices are deciding whether habeas corpus is the right procedure to challenge a change in custody level. His lawyer wants a broad rule, the government a narrower one, and a court-appointed lawyer argued habeas covers only release. Justices Gorsuch and Kagan pressed the lawyers, and Maxwell is due at a halfway house January twenty-second, raising a possible mootness question. A second case, Anderson versus Intel, asks what retirement plan participants must allege to sue.

Nick Eicher talks markets with financial analyst David Bahnsen on the Monday money beat. The Nasdaq lost ten percent last week, wiping out about four trillion dollars, and Anthropic's record-setting IPO was caught up in the drop. Bahnsen says more pain is possible, that nobody can know whether this is the bottom, and that people claiming to know are the ones to fear. He questions how these companies will make money, whether Nvidia's financing of customers and the neo-clouds hold up, and the dependence on Anthropic and OpenAI. He notes the stock traded five times its float in one day, and that OpenAI faces about one and a half trillion dollars in commitments. He adds that AI is promising, but past technology booms often rewarded later companies rather than early investors.

Bahnsen continues that AI is real and powerful but its commercial application was never clear, and like railroads, telecom and the internet, it will pay off slowly while many lose money. Asked about breaches such as the one at JPMorgan Chase, he says the bank is attacked thousands of times a day, that such problems get fixed, and that the benefits of financial technology outweigh the risks. He cites Y2K as a failed prophecy of doom. The hosts wish him a happy Thanksgiving. Then Emma Eicher begins a World History Book segment on Robert Stroud, the Birdman of Alcatraz, who died sixty-three years ago this week. Author Jolene Babiak describes his rough childhood, leaving home by thirteen, and a first killing at nineteen.

Stroud was jailed in 1909 and moved to Leavenworth after violence. In 1916 he killed a guard and was sentenced to life in solitary confinement. There he raised sparrows and canaries, published articles on bird diseases, and gained a following, and the warden gave him more privileges. He was later moved to Alcatraz, where he could keep no birds. A 1955 biography and the 1962 film with Burt Lancaster made him seem a gentle genius, but Babiak says the real Stroud was bombastic and threatening, and his research was rudimentary. He still wrote two books on bird diseases and is credited with a cure for one bacterial illness. He died in 1963 at seventy-three, after forty-two years in solitary. Tomorrow's show covers the Muslim Brotherhood and a zoo documentary.
